source.title: [Paper] Dictionary Learning Identifiability for Understanding SAEs

record.file_problem: This is a LessWrong summary, not the linked paper's full text. Some mathematical notation is missing from the post, and the referenced figures are not included.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports theoretical results that refine or challenge claims about feature hierarchies and splitting: its analysis says hierarchically dependent dictionary features cannot be stable optima, and that splitting continues in the wide-dictionary limit.
record.gate_note: The post reports theoretical conclusions and describes toy-data illustrations, but gives no quantitative outcomes for real SAEs. The cited prior work is not this study's evidence.
record.test_reason: A theoretical analysis of dictionary learning optimality conditions. It argues that hierarchically dependent features cannot be optima, that hierarchies become mutually exclusive features (splitting and absorption), and that splitting continues in the wide limit. It is a specific argument bearing on V1, V3, V4 and V6. It is not an original source, and its evidence is only theory plus toy data.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author derives first-order optimality conditions for dictionary learning. These prohibit hierarchically related features, frame splitting and absorption as converting hierarchies into mutually exclusive features, and show splitting continues in the wide limit. The author notes the work is largely theoretical, uses toy data and studies dictionary learning rather than SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes theoretical analysis of dictionary learning and its optimality conditions, rather than directly training and comparing SAEs of increasing sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: A 1D-data toy model and the wide-limit analysis are said to explain phenomena related to dense features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dense SAE features arise as a consequence of dictionary-learning optima in the wide limit.

record.problems: The post itself notes very limited experiments on real SAEs, a largely theoretical contribution tested on toy datasets, and that it studies dictionary learning rather than SAEs. The mathematical notation is missing in places and the referenced figures are absent from the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate numerical toy-data or real-SAE outcomes are stated in the post; the referenced illustrations are described without their figures or values.

untested.parts: No real SAE size comparison. Input coverage and directional nearness of the finer features are not shown.
Entire version: no large-model or open-SAE-release results.
Geometric closeness of feature families in real models is not measured.
No empirical measurement of parent and child firing. No SAE size or sparsity sweep; the claim that size doesn't fix absorption rests only on theory.
Entire version: no decomposition of larger latents into smaller ones, and no novel-latent analysis.
No comparison of SAE objectives and no test of Matryoshka SAEs. The analysis covers dictionary learning, not SAEs.

missing.what: Feature-residual necessary condition: an SAE with a dog feature cannot leave the labrador feature in the residual and is forced to mop it up.
Mutually exclusive features are always stable. Splitting and absorption are framed as two manifestations of converting a hierarchy into mutually exclusive features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong summary of arXiv 2606.02385; figures and notation are missing. All verdicts rest on theoretical arguments, not empirical SAE measurements, so their evidential weight is limited to the idealized dictionary-learning optimum.

versions.untested_parts: It does not directly compare SAE dictionary sizes trained on the same activations, or establish that finer features partition a coarse feature's inputs and lie near its direction.
No large-model or open-SAE-release results are reported.
The post does not measure geometric closeness or whether feature families mirror a model's concept hierarchy.
It does not measure parent and child firing patterns or test whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption.
It does not test whether larger latents decompose into smaller latents or whether larger dictionaries add novel latents.
The analysis concerns dictionary learning rather than SAEs themselves; it does not compare SAE objectives or test Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: dictionary learning

conditions.value: a lower-level feature is active only when a higher-level feature is active

rows.measure: Whether a hierarchically dependent feature pair can be a stable optimum
rows.value: The post says the relevant convex hull is empty, making the feature combination unstable and unable to be a minimum.
rows.note: The post presents this as a theoretical constraint on dictionary learning, illustrated with the dog/labrador hierarchy.
rows.check: The state 'absent' refers to stable nested parent/child pairs, which the theory rules out for V3. For V4 the same result predicts absorption: a hierarchy is turned into mutually exclusive features at any optimum. For V4 this row should read as consistent with the version, not as absence of the effect. The row should also be linked to V4, which the record omitted.

source_check.correct: Text: the hierarchy gives an empty convex hull, the combination is unstable and 'can never be a minima', and hierarchies are turned into mutually exclusive features. 'absent' fits only the V3 within-dictionary nested-pair part. For V4 and V6 this result is the predicted effect (absorption or splitting from the objective), so the state there is observed (theory).

statements.correction: The post presents arXiv:2606.02385 as its paper, so the two are the same work and not independent. The post says dictionary learning keeps splitting until each data ray has an atom. It notes very limited experiments on real SAEs.
statements.problem: 'May be the same work' is too weak. The post is the author's own summary of arXiv:2606.02385 and links it as 'The paper'. The necessary-not-sufficient remark is attributed to the arXiv paper, not to this post, so it is not an error here.
Only the R1 claim is about this study, and it is accurate. The 4 of 30 and 2 of 10 figures come from arXiv:2606.02385.
Makes no claim about this study.

statements.correction: Theory, vanilla dictionary learning: a child active only with its parent gives an empty convex hull, so the pair cannot be a minimum. Mutually exclusive features are always stable. Splitting and absorption turn a hierarchy into mutually exclusive features. Tested on toy data with very limited real-SAE experiments. Label: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The facts are right, but the 'challenges' label overstates the result. The theory rules out within-dictionary pairs where the child is active only with the parent. It frames splitting and absorption as turning a hierarchy into mutually exclusive features, which is consistent with split families that reflect a hierarchy. It does not address nesting across dictionary sizes.
